fields.foundation: The Safavid Empire was founded in 1501 by the fourteen-year-old Ismail I, head of the Safaviyya Sufi order based at Ardabil in north-western Iran. He led the Qizilbash, a confederation of Turkmen tribes (traditionally seven) named for their distinctive red headgear, to victory over the Aq Qoyunlu at the Battle of Sharur, seized Tabriz and proclaimed himself Shah. The Safaviyya order had been gathering religious prestige and a military following across north-western Iran and eastern Anatolia for some two centuries. It traced its spiritual lineage to the Sufi sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili (1252–1334), from whom the dynasty took its name. Ismail at once proclaimed Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, and no other act of his did more to decide later Iranian and Middle Eastern history. It was a radical imposition in a region that was predominantly Sunni and had little recent tradition of Shia rule at the state level. The declaration was a genuine religious commitment. It was also a means of building an Iranian political identity distinct from the Sunni Ottoman and Uzbek empires on either side, and a way to mobilise the intense devotion of Qizilbash warriors who believed Ismail to be a manifestation of the divine. Within a decade of taking Tabriz, Ismail had conquered the Iranian plateau, Iraq (including Baghdad in 1508) and parts of eastern Anatolia, and so unified a territory that had been politically fragmented since the break-up of the Mongol Ilkhanate in the fourteenth century. Three things made this possible: the weakness of the Aq Qoyunlu after Uzun Hasan's death in 1478, the cohesion of the Qizilbash tribal confederacy, and the messianic authority that Ismail's personal charisma gave him.
fields.socioeconomy: The Safavid economy had three main supports: taxation of the Iranian plateau's farming communities, long-distance trade along the Silk Road and Indian Ocean networks, and the royal silk monopoly that Shah Abbas I established in 1619 as a principal source of state revenue. Iranian agriculture depended on the qanat system of underground channels carrying water from mountain aquifers to lowland fields. It made cultivation possible across an otherwise arid plateau and supported a largely sedentary peasantry growing wheat, barley, rice in the Caspian lowlands, and cash crops including cotton and, most importantly for Safavid commercial strategy, silk in the Caspian provinces of Gilan and Mazandaran. In 1604–1605 Abbas I uprooted the merchant community of Julfa on the Aras river, and this deportation of Armenians to New Julfa, a suburb of his new capital Isfahan, was a deliberate economic policy. The Armenians had commercial networks reaching European markets and the linguistic and financial expertise to conduct the silk trade on terms favourable to the crown, including routes that bypassed Ottoman territory via Russia and the Persian Gulf. The silk monopoly sent revenue directly to the treasury and paid for Abbas I's military reforms, building programme and diplomacy. Isfahan under Abbas I became one of the wealthiest cities in the world, and its bazaars linked Indian Ocean imports such as spices, textiles and precious stones with European demand for luxury goods. In the early period the Qizilbash military aristocracy stood at the top of the social hierarchy. Abbas I deliberately restructured the state's institutions, and Persian bureaucratic families and the ghulam slave-soldiers progressively displaced them.
fields.military: The Safavid military changed fundamentally between the empire's founding and the reign of Shah Abbas I, and the cause was the hard lesson of the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514. There Sultan Selim I deployed artillery and musket-armed janissary infantry against the Qizilbash cavalry, whose leaders, by tradition, scorned firearms as unmanly. Ottoman firepower routed them in a single day and Tabriz was briefly occupied. The Safavids permanently lost Diyarbakir and much of Kurdistan and eastern Anatolia, and the myth of Ismail's invincibility, on which Qizilbash commitment had rested, was shattered. Ismail is said never to have led troops in battle again. For nearly eight decades the army remained dependent on Qizilbash tribal cavalry, which was inadequate against Ottoman firepower and politically dangerous because of its commanders' independent power bases. Shah Abbas I's reforms from the 1590s onwards created new corps of ghulam cavalry, musketeers (tofangchi) and artillerymen (topchi), paid directly from the royal treasury and loyal to the Shah and not to tribal chiefs. The English adventurers Robert and Anthony Sherley are traditionally credited with a part in these reforms, probably an exaggerated one. With the reformed army Abbas recovered Herat and Khorasan from the Uzbeks in 1598, retook Tabriz and Azerbaijan from the Ottomans between 1603 and 1607, expelled the Portuguese from Hormuz with English naval help in 1622, and seized Baghdad and most of Iraq in 1623–1624. These campaigns brought the empire to its greatest extent in the 1620s.
fields.governance: The Safavid administration combined Persian bureaucratic traditions inherited from pre-Islamic and medieval Iranian statecraft with the new religious authority of Twelver Shia Islam. In theory temporal and spiritual power were united in the Shah. In practice they were negotiated between the court, the Qizilbash military aristocracy, the Persian bureaucracy and an increasingly powerful Shia clergy. Civil affairs were directed by the grand vizier (later styled etemad al-dowleh), the religious establishment was supervised by the sadr, and the qurchi-bashi commanded the Qizilbash royal guard. Under Abbas I the ghulam system added a further power centre of slave-officials dependent on the Shah, a deliberate counterweight to the Qizilbash. Provincial government was divided between military governors (beglarbegi) and fiscal administrators (vazir). Strategically sensitive provinces such as Azerbaijan, Khorasan and Fars were held by Qizilbash chiefs in the early period and increasingly by ghulam officials, or converted into crown land, under Abbas I's centralising reforms. The legal system ran on two tracks: Sharia law, administered by Shia qadis appointed through the sadr, covered personal status, family law and religious matters, while customary royal law (urf) administered through royal courts dealt with criminal, commercial and administrative cases. The conversion of Iran to Twelver Shiism gave the clerical establishment (ulama) a place in government that grew significantly from the late seventeenth century. More activist clerics then sought direct influence over appointments, minority communities and public morality, a trend that peaked under Shah Sultan Husayn (r. 1694–1722).
fields.impact: The Safavid Empire's most consequential act was to turn Iran into a predominantly Twelver Shia society. This was done over the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries through compulsion, missionary activity, the recruitment of Arab Shia scholars from Jabal Amil in Lebanon and from Bahrain, and the gradual upbringing of successive generations in Shia practice and identity. The change created much of the sectarian geography of the modern Middle East. The Safavid-Ottoman rivalry turned the Sunni-Shia divide into a geopolitical fault line, and the repeated wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries produced frontiers that followed confession as much as strategy. The most durable was that of the Treaty of Zuhab of 1639, whose line broadly anticipates the modern Iran-Iraq border. Persian arts flourished under royal patronage in the period. The carpet-weaving of the court workshops reached its classical peak in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries and produced masterpieces such as the Ardabil carpet and the hunting carpets now in London, Vienna and Milan. In miniature painting the period produced first Tahmasp I's celebrated Shahnameh and later the single-page works of Reza Abbasi. Isfahan's ensemble of Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque and the Ali Qapu palace is one of the supreme achievements of Islamic urban design. In diplomacy the Safavids sought the help of European powers against the common Ottoman threat. They exchanged embassies with Venice, the Habsburgs, Spain and England from the late sixteenth century and set precedents for Iran's later dealings with the European state system.
fields.decline: The Safavid collapse between 1722 and 1736 grew out of weaknesses that Shah Abbas I's own reforms had built into the state. A succession of weak rulers hastened it, as did a religious rigidity that alienated much of the empire's diverse population. Abbas I's answer to the Qizilbash problem, a ghulam establishment loyal personally to the Shah, worked during his lifetime but concentrated everything in the person of the ruler. His suspicion of his own sons, one executed and others blinded, left no capable adult heir, and future princes were thereafter raised in the seclusion of the harem. His grandson Shah Safi (r. 1629–1642) began his reign by purging experienced generals, officials and royal relatives. His successors, Abbas II (r. 1642–1666) being a partial exception, proved less and less capable of meeting either military or political challenges. Decline quickened under Shah Sultan Husayn (r. 1694–1722). Early in his reign the influential cleric Muhammad Baqir Majlesi (d. 1699) promoted pressure on Sunnis, Sufis, Jews, Zoroastrians and Christians that alienated minority communities. In 1709 the Ghilzai Afghans of Kandahar, Sunnis resentful of Safavid rule, rose under Mir Wais Hotak. In 1722 his son Mir Mahmud Hotak, with perhaps 20,000 men, defeated a much larger Safavid army at the Battle of Gulnabad in March and began the Siege of Isfahan, which lasted some seven months. Sultan Husayn surrendered in October 1722 and personally placed the crown on Mahmud's head. The able commander Nader Quli Afshar later expelled the Afghans, defeated the Ottomans and ruled through puppet Safavid shahs. In 1736 he convened an assembly on the Mughan plain and had himself proclaimed Shah, formally ending the Safavid dynasty after 235 years.
fields.summary: The Safavid Empire gave Iran its Shia Islamic identity. The change was so thorough and so firmly set in the country's institutions that it outlived the dynasty by three centuries, and it still marks Iranian culture, statecraft and geopolitical orientation.
fields.teaser: The Safavids made Twelver Shia Islam Persia's state religion from 1501, forging the Shia identity of modern Iran and a lasting sectarian rivalry with the Ottomans. Their capital Isfahan became one of the world's most celebrated cities.
fields.t0: Founded in 1501 by the Sufi leader Ismail I, the Safavid Empire reunited Iran for the first time since the Mongol Ilkhanate.
fields.t1: By imposing Twelver Shia Islam it gave Iran its lasting religious identity and turned the Sunni-Shia divide into a frontier with the Ottomans.
fields.t2: Weak harem-raised shahs and religious intolerance left it open to an Afghan revolt; Isfahan fell in 1722 and the dynasty ended in 1736.
fields.dyk: After surrendering Isfahan in 1722, Shah Sultan Husayn personally placed the crown on the head of the Afghan conqueror Mir Mahmud Hotak.
